checked.found: Dated c. 1151 (estimate, not documented); described as the earliest morality play / only medieval musical drama with attributed text and music. 'Among the earliest' is safe.
Sources give the early 1360s, or 'between 1360 and 1365'; no firm date, and the 1364 coronation theory is abandoned. 1365 is only the latest bound.
Written for the 25 March 1436 consecration of Florence Cathedral, marking completion of Brunelleschi's dome. Description matches.
Published 1567 in Missarum liber secundus; composition date uncertain (1555-67). The clear-words legend is later and 'said to' hedges it correctly.

Year 1721 (dedication dated 24 March 1721) and Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt confirmed, but first results do not describe a job application: Bach was already Kapellmeister at Cothen and the Margrave had asked for compositions. 'In hopes of winning a job' is a common but contested claim. Also 'Margrave in Berlin' is loose (Berlin was his seat, title Brandenburg-Schwedt).
First (private) performances 29-30 April 1798 at Schwarzenberg Palace, public 1799; opens with 'Representation of Chaos'. Start year 1798 used.
Premiered 5 December 1830, Paris Conservatoire; programme has an artist poisoning himself with opium, dream visions and love obsession (Harriet Smithson).
Op. 28 published 1839, 24 preludes through all major and minor keys.
Op. 61 incidental music for A Midsummer Night's Dream premiered 14 October 1843 (Wikipedia dates composition 1842); Wedding March is No. 9. 1843 is the premiere year.
Choral version premiered 15 February 1867 in Vienna with the Men's Choral Society.
Premiered 3 March 1875, Opera-Comique, Paris; scandalised first audiences. Cigarette-factory setting is from the Merimee story.
First complete Ring cycle at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, 13-17 August 1876; theatre built for the purpose.
Premiered 1 February 1896, Teatro Regio, Turin (Toscanini); Mimi is a seamstress.
Complete premiere 9 November 1901 (partial movements 1900); written after depression treated by Dahl, to whom it is dedicated.
Suite bergamasque published June 1905 (composed c. 1890, revised); Clair de lune is the third movement.
Premiered 22 November 1928 (some give 20-21), Paris Opera, commissioned by and danced by Ida Rubinstein; snare drum ostinato.
Premiered 2 May 1936 in Moscow; each character is a different instrument.
Premiered 8 June 1937, Frankfurt; medieval Goliardic Latin/German poems, framed by O Fortuna.
Premiered 30 May 1962 for consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral; Latin Mass for the Dead interleaved with Wilfred Owen.
Premiered 25 July 1976, Avignon; about five hours without intermission; title refers to Albert Einstein.
Premiered 22 October 1987, Houston Grand Opera; depicts Nixon's visit to China with Pat Nixon and Madame Mao as roles.
